narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 69.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Being in the bottom decile, far below the average ranking of accepted students, signaled to the model that you may struggle with the demands of the bar exam. Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and similarly pulled the prediction toward failure; again you placed in the lowest decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential feature, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.00 it is modestly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, yet the model still saw this as a slight positive signal that slightly reduced the predicted risk of failure.

Taken together, the two very low class rankings outweighed the modest benefit of your GPA and led the model to conclude that the risk of failing the bar was too high for admission.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic performance and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking challenging courses, seeking tutoring, or enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program before reapplying. Improving your class rank and gaining stronger evidence of exam readiness can meaningfully change future predictions. (248 words)
